lines.text: Now the corner rule, on a route: two meters ahead, then one and a half left. Ninety degrees.
Step one: the switch radius, r. Forty centimeters, or forty percent of the shorter leg, whichever is smaller.
Forty percent of one and a half is sixty centimeters, so r is forty.
Step two: the turning circle touches the first leg r before the corner, and the second leg r after.
Its radius is big R. The right triangle at the corner gives: big R equals r over tangent of half the turn.
Half of ninety is forty-five, whose tangent is one. So big R is forty centimeters.
Step three: driving around a circle takes sideways acceleration: v squared over big R.
Keep that within our planned braking, six. So v is the square root of six times big R.
Together: the square root of decel times r, over tangent of half the turn.
Ninety degrees: the square root of two point four. One point five five meters per second.
Forty-five degrees: two point four one. A one hundred thirty-five degree hairpin: one point zero zero.
Under about seventeen degrees, it's capped at top speed. Under one degree, the code calls it straight.
In our simulator, routes with this rule were eleven to twenty-six percent faster than stop-and-go.
And they stayed within about twenty centimeters of the drawn lines.
